Guillaume de Machaut. The supreme figure of the Ars Nova, the new art movement, who lived around 1300 to 1377. He was a poet-composer whose sophisticated rhythmic innovation and intricate polyphony fundamentally transformed European medieval composition.

Machaut composed the Messe de Notre Dame, a four-voice polyphonic mass that unified the ordinary into a single cohesive work. This was a structural innovation that influenced how composers would approach the mass form for centuries. A key technique in his work was isorhythm: repeating rhythmic patterns combined with repeating melodic patterns in the tenor voice. This created architectural complexity that sat beneath the flowing upper melodies.

He wrote over one hundred forty secular songs including rondeaux, virelais, and lais, often setting his own refined love poetry to sophisticated rhythmic and harmonic language. He composed nineteen motets in which the isorhythmic technique reached its most sophisticated expression, balancing mathematical construction with emotional expressivity. Machaut served as a canon at Reims Cathedral and held positions in aristocratic courts, making him one of the first music composers to achieve secular prestige and documented fame. His work reveals a striking division: his motets are abstract and structurally complex, designed for the mind to follow, while his secular songs prioritize melodic grace and lyrical intimacy, designed for the heart. Together, these two sides of his output define what the Ars Nova achieved.
